newsitem.title: USA: U.S., France try to aid Zaire peace - Millon.
newsitem.headline: U.S., France try to aid Zaire peace - Millon.

text.p: The United States and France are trying to aid a peace agreement in Zaire, French Defence Minister Charles Millon said on Tuesday.

"Yes, there is a common U.S.-French approach as far as trying to reach peace and achieve a positive change, change toward stability in Zaire," he said before a meeting with U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen.

"The U.S. and France are coordinating their diplomacy so that (rebel leader Laurent) Kabila and Mobutu (President Mobutu Sese Seko) can reach an agreement on a government that will satisfy what the people expect from it," Millon said through an interpreter.

Cohen did not reply directly when asked if the United States and other countries were trying to help achieve a Zaire peace agreement, saying "obviously there are countries who are concerned about the situation in Zaire."

Defence Department spokesman Ken Bacon said U.S. helicopters and C-130 cargo planes were being sent to neighbouring countries along with about 600 U.S. troops in case the peace effort fails and Americans must be evacuated.

Bacon said Americans should be able to evacuate on boats across the Zaire River to Brazzaville in the Congo Republic. But he said the helicopter landing ship Nassau would arrive with 1,400 Marines on April 2 in case chaos prevented a boat evacuation and the Marines were needed to get Americans out.

The State Department said on Monday that Secretary of State Madeleine Albright had sent Mobutu a letter urging him to seek a ceasefire and establish a negotiating team or designate a person who can engage in negotiations on behalf of the Zaire government.

"We have consistently -- for some days if not weeks -- encouraged the government of Zaire and the rebel alliance, for that matter, to establish a ceasefire and to engage in dialogue," State Department spokesman John Dinger said.
He said that, basically, was what Albright's letter said.
Mobutu and Kabila have sent teams to Lome, Togo, for a special Organisation of African Unity summit starting Wednesday on the six-month war in Africa's third largest country.

Government sources in South Africa told Reuters that Kabila, leader of a rebel drive since October to topple Mobutu, had dropped a demand to negotiate only with Mobutu. But he has said he will only negotiate with Mobutu's representatives once and the outcome must be conclusive, according to the sources.
Millon said he and Cohen would discuss a number of subjects including a dispute over France's insistence that a European rather than an American command NATO southern forces.

The French minister did not comment on an Italian compromise proposal that a decision be deferred for at least five years but said "obviously in order to have a reinforced Atlantic alliance we need to have parity in this area."
